progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c16 (pH or amount; a probe gives pH, a titration gives total titratable acid; calibrate with two buffers close to the samples, ideally either side; clear and fast samples suit a direct titration); chem-m6-p06 (titration technique: rinse with what's going in, read at eye level to 0.05 mL, rough run then dropwise, concordant titres, error tracing); chem-m6-c12 (four steps, 1 : 1 for ethanoic acid with NaOH, NaOH is standardised because it absorbs water and CO₂); chem-m6-c13 (phenolphthalein suits a weak acid titrated with a strong base); chem-m6-c08 and c10 (weak acid pH from Ka; ethanoic acid Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵); chem-m6-p03 (meter routine: rinse, blot, read, record temperature); chem-m6-p04 (diluting a weak acid tenfold raises its pH by less than one unit; volumetric dilution); chem-m6-g03 (scale-up from an aliquot; percentage by mass needs a density); chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy, risk). Year 11: n = cV, n = m/M.
progression.startsWith: Choose a household sample, preparation and suitable analysis method. The video opens: A pH probe reads this white vinegar at two point four six. Dilute it ten times, and it reads two point nine six. Same vinegar, two different pH values, and neither one measures how much acid is in the bottle.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the two questions a household acidity analysis can answer and the measurement for each; measuring pH on the undiluted sample with a probe calibrated by buffers either side; estimating a titre from a label and choosing a dilution; diluting with volumetric glassware and explaining why the moles are unchanged; titrating with standardised base to the first faint pink lasting 30 s; calculating the concentration with the dilution factor; reporting grams per 100 mL as titratable acidity, as ethanoic acid, and comparing with the label; checking pH against concentration through Ka; stating the result's limits; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows; applying the method to an ammonia cleaner. No method tree (chem-m6-c16), no back titration (chem-m6-c15), no percentage uncertainty.

teaching.task: A pH probe reads the same white vinegar as 2.46 neat and 2.96 diluted tenfold, and neither number is the amount of acid in the bottle. How do you prepare, measure and report a household sample so that each number means what you say it means?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the same vinegar gives two pH values, and neither is an amount (1); (2) two questions need two measurements: pH for how acidic, a titration for how much; clear, fast vinegar suits a direct titration (2); (3) pH describes the solution the probe sits in, so it is measured on the undiluted sample, with buffers either side (3); (4) the label lets you estimate the titre before you start; neat vinegar would need more than three burette fills (4); (5) dilute the sample, not strengthen the base: stronger base is corrosive, and dilution keeps the moles, so you multiply back by ten (5); (6) the base is standardised because it absorbs CO₂; the endpoint is the first faint pink that lasts 30 s (6); (7) concordant titres give the mean (7); (8) 1 : 1 ratio, moles in the aliquot, concentration of the dilution, times ten (8); (9) report as the label does, grams per 100 mL, and compare (9); (10) two results with two meanings, consistent through Ka; the titration counts every acid, so "as ethanoic acid" (10); (11) the limits of the result (11); validity, reliability, accuracy (12); risk (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: a probe reads the same white vinegar at pH 2.46 neat and 2.96 diluted tenfold, and neither number is the amount of acid in the bottle, so the practical asks how to prepare, measure and report a household sample so that each number means what you say it means. Two questions need two measurements: pH for how acidic it is now, measured on the sample as it is with a probe calibrated by pH 7 and pH 2 buffers, and a titration for how much acid it holds. The titration is planned from the label's 4% so the titre fits the burette, and the vinegar is diluted tenfold rather than using a corrosive stronger base; the standardised sodium hydroxide, the concordant titres, the C12 calculation one line per stage and the conversion to grams per 100 mL follow, and the two results are shown to fit together through Ka. The limits of the result (one bottle, other acids, the endpoint), validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment close the method. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, the second on an ammonia cleaner left open on the bench.
teaching.openingDecision: A pH probe reads this white vinegar at two point four six. Dilute it ten times, and it reads two point nine six. Same vinegar, two different pH values, and neither one measures how much acid is in the bottle. So how do you analyse a household sample so that every number you report means what you say it means?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A cleaning vinegar is labelled '6% acidity', meaning 6 g of ethanoic acid per 100 mL. A student plans to titrate 25.00 mL aliquots of the undiluted cleaning vinegar with 0.09940 mol/L sodium hydroxide from a 50.00 mL burette. M(CH₃COOH) = 60.05 g/mol. Use the label to estimate the expected titre, and explain how the student should change the plan." Answer: about 1 mol/L; about 0.025 mol per aliquot; about 250 mL of base, five burette fills; dilute tenfold (25.00 mL to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask), giving titres of about 25 mL, then multiply by ten, or use a 2.50 mL aliquot of the neat vinegar (also about 25 mL of base; accepted). Crossed mistake: "just refill the burette five times" (each refill adds two readings and their error, and time). (A2) "A student analyses a household ammonia cleaner. She pours some of the cleaner into an open beaker and leaves it on the bench for 40 minutes. She then pipettes 25.00 mL of it into a 250.0 mL volumetric flask, makes it up to the mark, and titrates 25.00 mL aliquots with standardised hydrochloric acid using methyl orange indicator. All other steps are carried out correctly. Explain the effect of leaving the cleaner in the open beaker on her calculated concentration of ammonia in the cleaner." Answer: ammonia is a dissolved gas and some escapes from the open beaker, so her sample holds fewer moles of NH₃ than the bottle; less acid is needed; the titre is smaller; the calculated concentration is too low for the cleaner in the bottle. Crossed mistake: "water evaporates, so it becomes more concentrated and the answer is too high" (ammonia leaves the solution much faster than water does; author note i).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a chemical analysis of a common household substance for its acidity or basicity (ACSCH080)   , for example:; soft drink; wine; juice; medicine" this video prepares students to carry out and report a household acidity analysis; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: framing the analysis as two questions (how acidic now: pH; how much in total: titration), with C16's choice recalled in one clause; measuring the pH first, on the undiluted sample, with a probe calibrated by buffers either side of the sample, because pH describes the solution the probe sits in; planning the titration from the label (estimate the concentration and the titre before starting); diluting the sample tenfold rather than using a more concentrated, corrosive base; carrying out the titration (C12 and P06 technique recalled, not re-taught); the titre table and the calculation with the dilution factor; reporting on the label's basis (grams per 100 mL) as titratable acidity "as ethanoic acid"; checking that the pH and the concentration are consistent through Ka (C08 callback, one sentence); the limitations of the result; validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment. Basicity is applied in attempt 2 (an ammonia cleaner). Placement (playlist order 27): the last Chemistry Module 6 video, after C16 (order 26), G04 (order 25), C15 (order 24), C14, C13, G03 and P06. So indicator choice, the probe's calibration roles, the method tree and percentage by mass from density are all available as callbacks. Not re-taught: pH versus amount (C16, recalled as a two-question card); how a probe works and which buffer sets which parameter (C16); rinsing, meniscus reading, rough runs and error tracing (P06); the four-step titration calculation (C12); why phenolphthalein suits a weak acid with a strong base (C13); scale-up and percentage by mass (G03); weak acid pH from Ka (C08). Not here: back titration of an antacid (C15 and G03); red wine, soft drink and juice analyses (C16 tags; author note h); percentage uncertainty arithmetic; the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge scene (C16).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C12 and P06): the known solution's values (standardised NaOH) navy; the unknown's values (vinegar) amber; the ratio box teal; concordant titres ringed teal; pH values violet (a measurement of "how acidic", kept visually apart from amounts); the label's claim grey; limitations grey; controls green, hazards terracotta; phenolphthalein colourless and pink as painted. Board layout (three zones, constant, as P06): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus; the right third holds the current card (question card, reading table, plan, titre table, calculation, report, limitations, VRA, risk), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates, inspected 21 Oct on the dark board: `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (glass bottle with a cork-coloured cap; the painted liquid is pale gold, so the coded label "white vinegar, 4% acidity" carries the identity, as in C12; see Open decisions), `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (bench meter with a blank display, probe in a beaker; readout coded), `m6-burette-clamp-stand-v1.png`, `m6-conical-flask-v1.png`, `m6-white-tile-v1.png`, `m6-volumetric-flask-v1.png`, `m6-volumetric-pipette-filler-v1.png`, `m6-beaker-v1.png`, `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png`, `m6-clip-phenolphthalein-colourless-v1.png` and `m6-clip-phenolphthalein-pink-v1.png` (aligned pair, 2048 × 1700; the pink is pale, which suits "first faint pink"), `m6-household-cleaner-bottle-v1.png` (blue spray bottle; attempt 2 with the coded label "ammonia cleaner"), `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png` (risk). From P03's Codex asset brief (requested, not yet painted): `m6-buffer-bottle-v1.png` (scene 3; fallback below). Not used: `m6-red-wine-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` and `m6-red-wine-glass-v1.png` (C15 and C16 samples), `m6-lemon-v1.png` (juice is a C16 tag only), `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (owner rule). No human figures.
